blueprint_topic: Recognition of procedure-related complications and focused reassessment
stem: The day after a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure, a client develops new disorientation and asterixis. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: These findings are concerning for post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy and require prompt focused assessment and communication with the treating team.
options.B: These findings are an expected harmless effect of portal decompression and do not require evaluation unless they persist for several weeks.
options.C: These findings prove that the TIPS is occluded because hepatic encephalopathy occurs only when portal decompression has failed.
options.D: These findings are best explained by routine venous-access discomfort and are unrelated to the physiologic effects of portosystemic shunting.

rationale: A is correct. AASLD identifies hepatic encephalopathy as a well-known and clinically important complication after TIPS. TIPS redirects portal blood into the systemic circulation and reduces first-pass hepatic clearance of neurotoxins, so new disorientation and asterixis after the procedure are compatible with hepatic encephalopathy and warrant prompt assessment rather than reassurance. Current NCBI guidance also identifies TIPS and other portosystemic shunts as causes of hepatic encephalopathy and lists confusion, disorientation, altered attention, and asterixis among clinically relevant findings. B is incorrect because new neurologic changes are not a harmless expected finding to ignore. C is incorrect because hepatic encephalopathy can occur with a functioning TIPS and does not by itself prove shunt occlusion. D is incorrect because venous-access discomfort does not explain a new encephalopathic mental-status change and asterixis. The final item narrows the construct to one high-value post-TIPS complication instead of bundling encephalopathy, access-site bleeding, and shunt-patency surveillance into a single recall answer.
educational_objective: Recognize new confusion and asterixis after TIPS as possible post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy requiring prompt focused assessment and escalation rather than assuming a benign postprocedure effect or shunt occlusion.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD); National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), StatPearls

correction_summary: Rebuilt and remapped the source item. The original bundled post-TIPS monitoring answer and Safety/Infection Control mapping were too broad. The final item isolates a directly supported high-value complication—post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy—using new disorientation and asterixis, and maps it to Reduction of Risk Potential because the tested behavior is recognition and assessment of a procedure-related complication. Unsupported implications about mandatory timing or automatic shunt dysfunction were removed.
audit_findings: The original item bundled several different post-TIPS monitoring domains and was incorrectly mapped primarily to Safety and Infection Control.
Fresh AASLD review directly identifies hepatic encephalopathy as a well-known complication of TIPS and explains reduced hepatic first-pass clearance after shunting.
Fresh NCBI review independently supports TIPS as a cause of hepatic encephalopathy and the clinical relevance of disorientation and asterixis.
The final distractors exclude three realistic errors: dismissing new neurologic findings, equating HE with TIPS occlusion, and attributing the findings to routine access-site effects.
